title: MindGraph reproducible graph benchmark
subtitle: MindGraph, its exact ArcadeDB upstream control, and Neo4j Community measured on one BytePlus host; ArcadeDB website numbers remain contextual references.

summary: MindGraph, the exact ArcadeDB upstream commit, and Neo4j were executed sequentially on the same otherwise-idle host.
The graph comparison uses datagen-7_5-fb with 633,432 vertices and 34,185,747 edges; LSQB uses the same SF1 merged-FK source and exact Cypher queries from the pinned public harness.
MindGraph and upstream graph outputs are fingerprinted outside the timed region and must match before the report is marked verified.
Neo4j graph results are checked through complete-result semantic invariants for every algorithm and every run; all LSQB systems are checked against the nine official expected counts.

Graph algorithm timing reports five measured runs after one full warm-up. MindGraph and upstream LSQB report five measured runs; Neo4j LSQB reports three because each complete pass is substantially longer.
Data loading and Neo4j GDS projection construction are excluded from the timed query and algorithm regions.
disclosures: ArcadeDB published references came from arcadedb.com/benchmarks.html and were not measured on this host; its graph chart names graph500-22, so those values are context rather than an apples-to-apples comparison with datagen-7_5-fb.
The graph algorithm section uses the public harness native load-once runner, not an official LDBC audited result or certification.

MindGraph and upstream are embedded JVM measurements; Neo4j is a Docker server measured over Bolt and GDS Community is explicitly limited to four concurrent workers. The dashboard therefore labels Neo4j as a same-host competitor series, not a perfectly symmetric engine microbenchmark.
Neo4j LSQB Q9 exceeded 300 seconds. It is retained as a completed, count-validated result rather than censored or replaced by a timeout value.
These results are not application TPS, production sizing, or a claim that one system is universally faster.
The inherited OLTP-to-OLAP benchmark uses randomized graph generation, so speedup is directional rather than a deterministic conformance value.
